issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, there are numerous empty brackets or spaces where citations should be. This makes it impossible to verify the theoretical claims, historical context, and methodological precedents cited by the authors.
issues.quote: Sligte and colleagues have additionally suggested the presence of an intermediate form of STM, namely fragile memory , which, like WM, lasts at least 4 seconds, but unlike WM has a capacity of 5-15 items.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, pseudo-letter targets were present in the response options only 50% of the time, whereas real letter targets were present 83% of the time. This forces participants to choose 'none of these' or make an error much more frequently for pseudo-letter targets. If forced to guess, they may select the visually similar mirrored version, artificially inflating the 'illusory error' rate for pseudo-letters due to task design rather than true memory illusions.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials...

issues.subcategory: Massive exclusion based on dependent variable
issues.description: The authors excluded participants who had 10 or fewer 'high confidence' trials in any cell. This led to massive exclusion rates (42.5% in Exp 1, 31.7% in Exp 2). Excluding participants based on their confidence (a dependent variable) creates a severe selection bias, meaning the sample only represents highly confident individuals, severely limiting generalizability and potentially skewing the error rates.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The authors state that confidence was rated on a scale from 1 to 4, and then base their entire analysis and participant exclusion criteria on 'high confidence trials'. However, they never define which ratings (e.g., just 4, or 3 and 4) constitute 'high confidence'. This makes the study impossible to replicate and the results difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain)... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials...

issues.subcategory: Unreported statistical tests for low confidence trials
issues.description: In the Discussion of Experiment 1, the authors make specific claims about the error rates in low confidence trials to argue against a response bias. However, the data, statistical tests, and exact methodology for analyzing these low confidence trials are never reported in the Results section.
issues.quote: On high confidence trials pseudo-letter targets were more often confused for their real counterparts (36%) than on low confidence trials (22%). However, the reverse was observed when real letter targets were confused for their pseudo counterpart (high confidence: 11%, low confidence: 17%).

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the authors state that participants with 10 or fewer high confidence trials in any cell were excluded. In the very next sentence, they state that one participant was excluded due to listwise deletion because they had 0 high confidence responses in a cell. If the first rule was applied, no participant with 0 responses could possibly remain in the dataset to be excluded by the second rule.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 59 participants (5 participants were excluded)... Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: Logically contradictory statement about effect sizes
issues.description: In Experiment 4, the authors state there was a 'smaller increase' for mirrored targets (5%) compared to real letter targets (4%). Since 5% is larger than 4%, this statement is logically contradictory and misrepresents the data.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: In the General Discussion, the authors claim that memory was probed at 500 ms in Experiments 1 and 2. However, the short delay in Experiment 1 was 0.75 seconds (750 ms), not 500 ms. This misrepresents the timeline of the memory decay tested in the first experiment.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous calculation of baseline error rates
issues.description: The response screen contains 6 options: 1 target, 1 mirrored counterpart (illusory error), and 4 other letters (other errors). It is never explicitly stated whether the 'other error' rate reported (e.g., 11%) is the sum of all 4 distractor options or the average per distractor. This ambiguity makes it difficult to evaluate whether the illusory error rate is genuinely higher than chance compared to the distractors.
issues.quote: while the other (non-illusory) error rate was not influenced by target-type (11% for real-letter and pseudo-letter targets)

issues.subcategory: Missing prior specifications for sequential Bayes Factors
issues.description: In Experiments 3 and 4, the authors used a sequential Bayes Factor design with a stopping rule of BF > 10. However, they do not specify the prior distribution used for the Bayesian t-test. The choice of prior is critical in Bayes Factor sequential designs as it directly impacts the trajectory of the BF and the probability of stopping.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.description: The authors state that 5 out of 45 participants were excluded based on training scores, and then claim this is 'only 10%'. 5 out of 45 is exactly 11.1%, not 10%.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results... Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores...

issues.description: In Experiment 4, the authors report a BF = 4.84 for the increase in non-illusory errors from short to long delays, and describe it as 'only increased from 6% to 7%'. According to standard Bayesian interpretation guidelines (which the authors themselves provided in Exp 1), a BF of 4.84 indicates substantial evidence FOR the alternative hypothesis. Framing it as a negligible effect downplays a statistically supported increase.
issues.quote: while the other non-illusory error rate only increased from 6% to 7% (BF = 4.84 in a follow up t-test).

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the authors tested for the effect of cue color, found it non-significant, and then collapsed across it. However, the exclusion criteria (<=10 trials per cell) was applied 'when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.' If they excluded based on the collapsed cells, they changed the definition of a 'cell' post-hoc based on the null result of the cue color analysis, which is a form of data-dependent analysis pipeline.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.
